summary: Extends MPLS LSP ping so the echo reply return path can be selected, to verify bidirectional connectivity and make it more robust. This makes LSP ping more flexible as a diagnostic tool.

plainLanguage.summary: When you ping, you can choose the road for the reply.

questions: what is the lsp ping reply path tlv
what is reply via specified path
how to test both directions of an mpls lsp
subtitle: Lets the sender of an MPLS LSP ping choose which path the echo reply must take back.

tldr.problem: LSP ping reports a path as down if the echo reply is lost, even when the path under test works. Testing both directions of a bidirectional LSP also meant logging on at each end and running two tests.
tldr.mechanism: A new Reply Mode, Reply via Specified Path, and a new Reply Path TLV let the sender say how the egress must send the reply: along a given LSP or tunnel, along the reverse of a bidirectional LSP, or along any non-default path.
tldr.outcome: One LSP ping can check both directions and can avoid an unreliable default return path. It is updated by RFC 7737.

today: RFC 7110 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 7737. It has not been obsoleted. The RFC itself limits its procedures to ping mode.

sections.title: What the Extension Adds
sections.content:
LSP ping, defined in RFC 4379, detects data-plane failures on MPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs). This RFC extends it so the sender can specify the return path of the echo reply. It adds a new Reply Mode, Reply via Specified Path, and a new Reply Path (RP) TLV.

The procedures apply only to "ping" mode. "Traceroute" mode is out of scope. They apply to both IP/MPLS and MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) scenarios, and to bidirectional LSPs, both co-routed ones and associated ones built from a pair of unidirectional LSPs.
sections.plainLanguage: Ping asks 'are you there?' along a road. This lets the asker say which road the answer must come back on.

sections.title: Problems With the Existing Reply Modes
sections.content:
Operators increasingly run bidirectional LSPs and want to test both directions in one operation. With RFC 4379 they have to enable detection at each end independently, which doubles the work. The router they are logged on to might not have out-of-band connectivity to the far end, so checking the return direction can mean logging on to the other router.

There is also a reliability problem. RFC 4379 defines four Reply Modes: do not reply, reply via an IPv4/IPv6 UDP packet, reply via a UDP packet with Router Alert, and reply via an application level control channel. The Router Alert mode needs every intermediate node to support the option, which is a rigorous requirement, and no UDP mode can guarantee delivery through an unreliable IP network. A lost reply produces a false negative: the LSP looks failed although it works.

Letting the ingress control the reply path makes the test more deterministic. For example, if a Mode 2 test gets no reply, the operator can retry with the new mode and a different return path believed to be workable.
sections.plainLanguage: If your friend's answer gets lost on a bad road, you might think they left. Choosing a good road for the answer fixes that.

sections.title: The Reply Path TLV
sections.content:
The new Reply Mode has value 5. When it is requested, the Reply Path TLV (type 21) MUST be in the echo request, and its absence is a malformed echo request. If a Reply Path TLV is in a request, a conformant implementation MUST include one in the reply.

The TLV holds a 2-octet type, a 2-octet length, a 2-octet Reply Path return code, 2 octets of Flags, and a variable Reply Path made of zero or more Target FEC sub-TLVs. In a request the return code must be zero. In a reply, it tells how the egress handled the request.

Two flag bits steer the choice. A (Alternative path) makes the egress pick a non-default path, useful when problems on the default reverse path are suspected. B (Bidirectional) requires the reply to follow the reverse direction of the tested bidirectional LSP. With either bit set, sub-TLVs are unnecessary and SHOULD be ignored. If both are set, the egress MUST return the code Malformed Reply Path TLV was received.
sections.plainLanguage: The request carries a note saying how to answer: use this road, use the road back, or use any road except the usual one. The answer carries a note saying what the replier did.

sections.title: Tunnel Sub-TLVs and the Reply TC TLV
sections.content:
The Reply Path can carry any Target FEC sub-TLV that RFC 4379 already defines, so a particular LSP can be named as the return path. This RFC also defines three new sub-TLVs for naming a more generic tunnel instead of one LSP: IPv4 RSVP Tunnel (type 26), IPv6 RSVP Tunnel (type 27) and Static Tunnel (type 28). Naming the tunnel avoids the effect of an LSP identifier changing when Make-Before-Break is used. The sub-TLV space for the Reply Path TLV is the same as for TLV type 1.

Each new sub-TLV has a Flags field with two bits. P (Primary) requires the return LSP to be the primary LSP of the tunnel, and S (Secondary) requires the secondary LSP. Both set is malformed. With neither set, any LSP of the tunnel may be used.

The Reply TC TLV (type 22, length fixed at 4 octets) may be used by the requester to ask that the reply go out with the Traffic Class bits of the return LSP set to a chosen value. It may be used with the other Reply Modes too.
sections.plainLanguage: You can point at one road, or at a whole highway with a main lane and a spare lane, and you can ask for the reply to travel in the fast lane.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Requests and Replies
sections.content:
To send a request, the ingress sets the Reply Mode to Reply via Specified Path and includes a Reply Path TLV. For a bidirectional LSP, only the B bit SHOULD be set. To use a different path, set the A bit or carry another FEC sub-TLV, with B clear. To test two unidirectional LSPs as a pair, the request MUST carry a FEC sub-TLV that belongs to the backward LSP.

The egress that does not know the new mode replies with the return code Malformed echo request received and subcode zero. One that knows it should find the desired path and send a reply with a Reply Path TLV and a fitting return code: success, specified path not found and another LSP used, or not found and plain IP forwarding used. An unknown sub-TLV gets its own code. The forward-path FEC validation result SHOULD NOT stop the egress from testing the return path.

When the reply travels over an MPLS LSP, the destination IP address is set from the range 127/8 for IPv4 or 0:0:0:0:0:FFFF:127.0.0.0/104 for IPv6, the IP TTL is set to 1, and the TTL of the outermost label is set to 255, so the destination address is never used for forwarding. The reply carries the return path's FEC stack so the ingress can validate it, which lets one ping test both directions. If the return path is plain IP, the RFC 4379 procedures apply unchanged. On receipt of a failure code, the operator may retry with another path or one of the four older modes.
sections.plainLanguage: The replier sends its answer along the chosen road with a stamp that stops it from wandering. The asker checks the road the answer used, so one trip tests both directions.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4379 apply. In addition, the extension could be used for "proxying" attacks, because a requester can specify a return path whose destination differs from the requester. The RFC notes this is not expected inside an MPLS domain where initiators and receivers belong to the same domain.

As a precaution, the return path LSP should end at the same node the forward path came from. The receiver may drop an echo request when it cannot tell whether the return path reaches the initiator, so the initiator should choose a source address that fits the specified return path.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could ask for the answer to be sent to a stranger. So the replier may refuse when it cannot tell the road leads back to the asker.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned TLV types 21 (Reply Path) and 22 (Reply TC) in the LSP ping parameters registry, sub-TLV types 26, 27 and 28 in the registry of sub-TLVs for TLV types 1, 16 and 21, and Reply Mode 5. Sub-types for the Target FEC Stack TLV and the Reply Path TLV must be kept the same.

IANA also created a new subregistry for Reply Path return codes. Values 0x0006 to 0xfffb are unassigned and allocated by Standard Action, and 0xfffc to 0xffff are for experimental use.
sections.plainLanguage: Official number labels were handed out so everyone uses the same number for each new message part.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length in octets of the return code, Flags and Reply Path fields.

fields.name: Reply Path return code
fields.desc: Zero in a request; filled in by the egress in a reply.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Must be zero except the A and B bits. A variable Reply Path of sub-TLVs follows.

items.label: Malformed
items.desc: Malformed Reply Path TLV was received.

items.label: Not understood
items.desc: One or more sub-TLVs were not understood.

items.label: Success
items.desc: The echo reply was sent using the specified Reply Path.

items.label: Other LSP
items.desc: Specified path not found; the reply was sent via another LSP.

items.label: Pure IP
items.desc: Specified path not found; the reply was sent via pure IP forwarding.
